name: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II
objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity, with oxygen lowered by nitrogen dilution of the glovebox.
ai_summary: BASS-II burned PMMA rods, sheets and slabs and a cotton-fiberglass fabric in a small flow duct inside the ISS glovebox, varying airflow (0 to 55 cm/s) and oxygen (21% and below). Its central fire-safety result is that materials can keep burning at lower oxygen in microgravity than in normal gravity. It also showed that flames always went out when the fan was switched off, supporting the ISS practice of shutting down ventilation when a fire is detected.

name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire I–VI)
platform: Cygnus cargo vehicle (uncrewed, after ISS departure)
facility: Saffire Flow Unit + Far Field Diagnostics
objective: Observe large-scale fire growth and spread on thin and thick solid fuels in long-duration microgravity, including the reduced-pressure, elevated-oxygen atmospheres planned for exploration spacecraft, and measure the fire's impact on the vehicle.
ai_summary: Saffire burned samples up to about 94 cm long inside an orbiting Cygnus spacecraft, the first practical-scale spacecraft fire tests. Flames reached a steady size and spread rate rather than growing without limit as they tend to on Earth. Saffire V and VI tested exploration-like atmospheres down to about 54 kPa and up to about 31% oxygen, the closest flight evidence to planned Moon and Mars habitat conditions.

name: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction – Material Ignition and Suppression Test
objective: Map ignition and extinction boundaries of PMMA cylinders as a function of flow speed, oxygen concentration, pressure and external radiant heating, with emphasis on NASA's proposed space exploration atmospheres.
ai_summary: SoFIE-MIST burned acrylic (PMMA) rods in the Combustion Integrated Rack at pressures down to 60 kPa. Researchers report the limiting oxygen concentration in microgravity is about 15%, compared with about 18% in normal gravity. That means materials judged non-flammable on Earth may burn in a spacecraft, and added external heating may lower the limit further.

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)
facility: Combustion Integrated Rack (Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus)
objective: Study how isolated burning fuel droplets extinguish in microgravity across oxygen levels, pressures and diluents (nitrogen, carbon dioxide, helium), to inform fire suppression for spacecraft.
ai_summary: FLEX burned single heptane and methanol droplets 1.5–5 mm across at 0.7–3.0 atm and 10–40% oxygen. It measured the oxygen levels below which droplets will not burn and showed how extinction size shifts as oxygen is reduced. It also discovered that large heptane droplets keep burning with an invisible 'cool flame' after the visible flame goes out, so a fire that looks extinguished may not be.

name: ACME – Burning Rate Emulator (BRE)
objective: Use a gas-fed porous burner with embedded heat-flux gauges to emulate the burning of solid and liquid materials, and map which materials can burn steadily in microgravity at different oxygen levels and pressures.
ai_summary: BRE emulated burning solids with ethylene/nitrogen flames on 25 and 50 mm porous burners at 21–40% oxygen and 0.56–1 bar, including NASA habitat atmospheres. Every flame in 21% oxygen self-extinguished within 40 seconds, while steady flames were achieved at 26.5%, 34% and 40% oxygen. Flame lifetimes scale strongly with oxygen fraction and were independent of pressure, which the researchers cite as further evidence of the hazard of oxygen-enriched spacecraft atmospheres.

name: Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G)
objective: Produce and study steady, spherical non-premixed cool flames burning gaseous fuel in microgravity, without the heated reactants ground tests require.
ai_summary: CFI-G produced the first steady spherical cool diffusion flames burning a gaseous fuel (n-butane), on June 23, 2021. The cool flames were too faint to see in real time and were found afterwards in radiometer and burner-temperature data. They appeared when residual heat in the burner re-ignited flowing fuel after the hot flame had gone out, a reignition path relevant to judging whether a fire is truly extinguished.

name: Structure and Liftoff in Combustion Experiment (SLICE)
objective: Measure the shape, liftoff, stability and soot of laminar coflow methane jet flames in microgravity and normal gravity to test combustion models.
ai_summary: SLICE burned nitrogen-diluted methane jet flames in an air coflow inside the ISS glovebox, from weak near-extinction flames to strongly sooting ones. Without buoyancy the flames were noticeably longer than their Earth counterparts, and soot shifted from the flame centerline toward its edges. These data mainly support model validation, with indirect relevance to smoke production and fire detection.
